title: Your first automatic flow in n8n
promise: You're going to have n8n open on your screen. You'll build a flow with three boxes that triggers itself every morning at 8:00. And you'll pick up a habit: checking the input and output columns of each box. That way you'll know in two minutes why something broke.
why: Rocío Cuevas restores furniture in Zaragoza and buys her hardware from a supplier in Ohio who bills her in dollars. Every morning she'd open the browser, check the exchange rate, and write it down by hand in a notebook before drawing up quotes. One Thursday in March she copied the number from three weeks earlier. She quoted a dresser with an old exchange rate and ate a €140 difference. What fixed the problem wasn't more discipline. It was three boxes drawn on a screen. Those boxes do the lookup for her at 8:00, every day, even the ones she's on vacation.

theory.title: n8n is a board where you draw what you already do by hand
theory.text: n8n is pronounced 'en-eight-en' and it's a blank screen where you place boxes and connect them with arrows. Each box is called a node (node: one step in the process) and does exactly one thing. It can check the time, ask another program for a piece of data, decide whether a number is over 500, or send an alert. The whole drawing, with all its boxes, is called a flow (workflow: the complete process saved under a name). The first box is always special and is called a trigger (trigger: what decides when everything starts). It can be a fixed time, an email arriving, someone filling out a form, or you clicking a button. When the flow runs start to finish, from the first box to the last, that's called an execution (execution). That's the unit you get billed by: twenty boxes still count as one execution. The doubt that comes up now is whether this is coding in disguise. The honest answer is: halfway. You don't write code, but you do think like someone who does. You have to decide the order, what happens if the data doesn't arrive, and who checks the result. What you save is the syntax; what you don't save is the thinking.
theory.analogy: It's the belt on an assembly line. Each worker makes one motion and pushes the piece to the next one. You don't build anything with your hands: you place the workers in the right order and press the green button.
theory.example: Rocío's flow is three boxes: 'at 8:00', 'ask what the dollar is worth' and 'write the sentence with the number'. Three boxes, one execution a day, thirty executions a month out of the 2,500 that come with the cheapest paid plan.

theory.title: Data travels in a card called JSON, and that's 80% of the lesson
theory.text: Between one box and the next, what travels isn't an image or a file: it's a data card with labels and values. That format is called JSON (pronounced 'jay-sahn'). A card is literally this: {"base": "USD", "date": "2026-08-18", "rates": {"EUR": 0.9174}}. You read it left to right as if you were dictating it: label 'base', value 'USD'. Then label 'rates', and inside another card with the label 'EUR' and the value 0.9174. Each node receives a card, changes it, and hands another card to the next one. n8n shows you both on screen. The INPUT column on the left is what arrived; the OUTPUT column on the right is what came out. Here's the only repair technique you need. If box 3 fails, don't search the internet: look at what came out of box 2. 80% of first-day failures come from expecting a piece of data that never arrived. You can see that in two seconds by comparing those two columns. And no, you don't have to learn to write JSON: just to read it, which is like knowing how to read an ingredients label without knowing how to cook.
theory.analogy: It's a patient's chart moving from one consultation to the next. Each doctor adds a line and passes it on to the next one. If the orthopedist complains that the X-ray is missing, the problem isn't the orthopedist: it's the earlier consultation.
theory.example: To grab the 0.9174 from that card you write {{ $json.rates.EUR }}. The $json sign means 'the card that arrived at this box'. Each dot goes down one level: first you go into rates, then you grab EUR. If you write {{ $json.EUR }} you'll get 'undefined', which means 'there's nothing here'.

theory.title: Where your n8n lives: in their cloud or on your computer
theory.text: n8n isn't an app you download to your phone. It's a program that has to stay running on some computer so it can watch the clock. There are two reasonable paths. The first is their cloud: you go to n8n.io, create an account, and two minutes later you have n8n open without installing anything. The trial is 14 days free and doesn't ask for a card. After that, the cheapest plan runs around €20-25 a month, with about 2,500 executions and five flows running at once. The second is your own computer: the license is free forever. But you have to paste a line into the terminal (the black screen where you type commands). And above all, your 8:00 flow will only fire if the computer is on and n8n is open at that hour. That almost never happens. There's a third path: renting a server for €5-10 a month and leaving n8n there. But that means maintaining it yourself, and that's not for today. The scary question is whether starting in the cloud locks you in. It doesn't: a flow downloads as a file and uploads to another n8n in two clicks. If you handle client data that by contract can't leave your company, the decision is already made. It goes on your machine.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between renting a spot in a garage with a 24-hour guard and parking on your street. Parking on the street is free, but you only have a car while you're there watching it.
theory.example: Rocío started with the cloud's free trial. Her flow uses 30 executions a month; the Starter plan brings 2,500. She has room for eighty flows like hers before paying an extra cent. Prices change every few months, so check the pricing page the day you're about to sign up.

theory.title: Save, test, and activate are three different buttons, and the one that'll trip you up is the third
theory.text: The Save button saves the drawing, and nothing else: it doesn't run it or turn it on. The Test workflow button, at the bottom center, makes it run once right now in front of you. It's for watching the boxes turn green one by one. The Active switch, top right, is the one that leaves the flow turned on so the trigger fires on its own when it's supposed to. The classic first-day accident is this: you build the flow, test it, it works, and you walk away happy. A week later you find out it hasn't run even once. Because testing isn't activating. There's a nuance that costs whole afternoons: a flow with a manual trigger can never be activated, because there's nothing to wait for. If you want it to fire on its own, the trigger has to be a schedule or an event. A webhook also works (an internet address your flow sits there listening on). And if you use a webhook, n8n gives you two addresses that look almost identical. One has the word 'test' in the middle; the other doesn't. The test one only listens while you have the screen open. If you paste it into a real service, nothing will arrive and you won't see any error anywhere.
theory.example: The switch is top right and by default says 'Inactive'. Click it and it turns green and changes to 'Active'. A window pops up explaining that from now on the flow runs on its own and executions will show up in the Executions tab. In the Overview list, your active flows carry a green tag; the rest, gray.

theory.title: n8n has no undo button over the real world
theory.text: Inside the editor you can undo with Ctrl+Z as much as you like, and that's deceptive. Outside the editor there's no going back. A sent email doesn't come back, and neither does a published message. A deleted row in a spreadsheet doesn't come back, and neither does a triggered order or payment. The rule that saves you the headache is simple and non-negotiable: while you're testing, you are the recipient. Your email, your number, a chat channel you've created for testing. The second rule is to set a cap while you're learning. The most expensive mistake a beginner makes isn't getting a field wrong. It's accidentally building a flow that calls itself. That flow fires off five thousand executions in three minutes, with five thousand emails behind it. And there's a third point that's about security. Passwords and access keys to other services get saved once inside a credential (the key kept separately). n8n encrypts it and it doesn't show up inside the drawing when you share it. But watch out if you type a key by hand into a regular text field. That key does travel inside the file the day you send it by email. Then the only fix is to revoke it and generate another.
theory.example: The typical case: a welcome flow to 4,200 contacts. Someone activates it on a Friday at 18:00 so it runs over the weekend. If the text has a typo, it's gone out to 4,200 people and there's no button that gets them back. The right sequence is to send it to yourself first, then limit it to ten test contacts, and only then let it go.

theory.title: AI builds your flow for you, but it doesn't press the buttons
theory.text: An n8n flow is text underneath, and that gives you a huge shortcut if you've never coded. You describe to Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini what you want and ask for the flow as text. You copy it, click on the empty canvas, and press Ctrl+V. The boxes appear drawn and connected, and all you have to do is open them and review. Where AI is really good: writing you the exact expression to pull a piece of data out of the card, and translating the red error message for you. Also at suggesting which boxes you need and in what order, from a plain-language description of yours. Where it'll trip you up: it invents names for nodes and fields that don't exist in your version, with total confidence. It does that because the tool changes faster than what it knows gets updated. So it's worth always asking it to use only basic nodes. And, if it's not sure about a parameter, to leave it at its default value instead of making it up. And there's something it can't do no matter how well you ask. It can't create your account, connect your Gmail, or flip the Activate switch. That part is yours, and that's why this lesson is about concrete buttons.
theory.example: Rocío asked Claude for the whole flow, pasted it onto the canvas, and the three boxes appeared. Two were perfect; the third had a made-up field showing up in red with a warning triangle. She deleted it, built it by hand in forty seconds, and moved on. Total: five minutes instead of twenty.

tasks.title: Decide where your n8n is going to run before you touch anything
tasks.where: In your head, with the browser open on n8n.io
tasks.action: There are only two reasonable answers today. (A) Their cloud: you go to n8n.io, create an account, and in two minutes you have n8n in front of you without installing anything. It's a 14-day trial, no card, and after that about €20-25 a month. (B) Your own computer: free forever, but you have to paste a line into the terminal. Plus, the flow only runs while the computer is on and n8n is open. Answer three questions out loud. Do I want it to fire at 8:00 even if my laptop is closed? Does it pay off for me to spend €25 a month if it takes two hours off my plate? Do I handle client data that by contract can't leave my computer? If the first two are yes, go to the cloud. If the third is yes, go with your computer.
tasks.prompt: I want to start using n8n and I'm not sure whether to use the cloud version or install it on my computer. My situation: [describe your work in two lines], [how many automations you think you'll have in six months], [whether you need them to run overnight or with the computer off], [whether you handle personal client data], [how much you're willing to pay per month]. I've never coded and the terminal makes me nervous. Give me a clear recommendation, one of the two, without saying 'it depends', with three concrete reasons for my case and a euro figure for what it would cost me monthly. Then tell me in one line what I lose with the option I skip and whether it's easy to switch later. Don't give me the installation tutorial yet.
tasks.expect: One sentence written on paper or in a note: 'going with the cloud' or 'going with my computer'. Nothing more.
tasks.stuck: If you're still unsure after five minutes, go with the cloud and don't overthink it. Moving later just means downloading a file from the three dots '...' on the flow and uploading it to the other place. No one has ever lost a flow by starting in the cloud.

tasks.title: Open n8n and reach the main screen
tasks.action: If you're going with the cloud: go to n8n.io and click the 'Get started for free' button in the top right. Enter an email and password, or sign in with Google. It'll ask your name and what you'll use it for (answer whatever, it's only used to show you templates). At some point it'll let you choose a region: if it gives you the option, pick Europe. When it's done it creates your own address with your name in it, something like https://rociocuevas.app.n8n.cloud. At the top you'll see a notice with the trial days you have left. If you're going with your computer: download Docker Desktop from docker.com (free, about 600 MB). Install it, open it, and wait for the whale icon to stop moving. Open the terminal (on Windows search for 'PowerShell' in the start menu; on Mac, 'Terminal'). Paste this whole line and press Enter: docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n . The first time it takes two or three minutes downloading things. When it stops and you see a line saying 'Editor is now accessible via: http://localhost:5678', open that address in the browser. It'll ask you to create a user with an email and password: that stays inside your computer, it's not an internet account. While the black window stays open, n8n is on; if you close it, it turns off.
tasks.expect: The Overview screen: a narrow bar on the left with 'Overview', 'Personal' and 'Templates'. The center will be empty or show a welcome message. And at the top right, an orange button that says 'Create Workflow'. If you see that orange button, you've got n8n.
tasks.stuck: In the cloud: if the confirmation email doesn't arrive, check the spam folder before registering again. A second attempt with the same email throws an error. On your computer: if the terminal says something about 'port is already allocated', 5678 is taken. Change the start of the line to -p 5679:5678 and go to http://localhost:5679. If it says 'cannot connect to the Docker daemon', Docker Desktop isn't open: open it, wait for the whale to sit still, and try again. And if you closed the black window by accident, just paste the same line again: your saved flows are still there.

tasks.title: Learn the four zones of the screen before you draw anything
tasks.where: In n8n, on the Overview screen
tasks.action: Take a one-minute tour without clicking anything important. On the left: 'Overview' is the list of all your flows and 'Personal' is your folder. 'Templates' are flows already built by others that you can copy. And at the very bottom is your initial, with 'Settings' inside. The orange 'Create Workflow' button is top right. Now open any flow, or create one, and look at the four things you'll use all the time. Top left is the flow's name: by default it says 'My workflow' and you change it by clicking on it. Top center there are two tabs: 'Editor' (the drawing) and 'Executions' (the history of times it's run). Top right are the 'Save' button, the switch that says 'Inactive', and the three dots '...'. Inside the three dots are Import, Download, Duplicate, Delete and Settings. And at the bottom center, the 'Test workflow' button. The rest of the screen is the canvas: the gray dotted area where you place the boxes. You move it by dragging with the mouse and zoom with the scroll wheel.
tasks.expect: You can point, without looking for them, to the four spots: where you save, where you turn it on, where you see the history, and where you test.
tasks.stuck: n8n is in English and has no official translation, so learn these five. Save is guardar, Executions is ejecuciones and Active is encendido. Test workflow is probar el flujo and Delete is borrar. If your screen doesn't quite match this description, your version has moved some button around. The four that matter are still top right and bottom center.

tasks.title: Create the flow and give it a name that'll make sense in six months
tasks.action: Click the orange 'Create Workflow' button top right. An empty canvas opens with a dashed box in the center and a big '+' sign. Before drawing anything, go top left where it says 'My workflow'. Click on the text (it becomes editable), delete it, and type: Dollar-euro rate every morning. Press Enter. Now click the orange 'Save' button top right. This step looks trivial and it isn't. Six months from now you'll have nine flows. If three are called 'My workflow 2', you won't know which ones you can delete and which one emails clients. So you won't dare touch any of them.
tasks.expect: The name you typed appears top left, and the orange 'Save' button has changed to gray text that says 'Saved'. If you go back to Overview with the back arrow, your flow shows up in the list with today's date.
tasks.stuck: If the 'Save' button is still orange, it hasn't saved. Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on Mac). If you get a warning about unsaved changes when trying to leave, tell it to stay and save first. And if the name won't let you type, you probably clicked next to it instead of on it: aim right at the word.

tasks.title: Place the trigger: the box that starts everything else
tasks.where: In n8n, on the canvas of your new flow
tasks.action: Click the dashed box in the center that says 'Add first step…'. A panel opens on the right titled 'What triggers this workflow?'. Below it is a list: 'Trigger manually', 'On app event', 'On a schedule', 'On webhook call', 'On form submission', 'On chat message', and a few more. Choose the first one, 'Trigger manually'. The panel closes on its own and a box appears on the canvas with a lightning icon and the text 'When clicking Test workflow'. We're starting with the manual trigger on purpose: while you're building, you want to press a button and see the result instantly. We'll add the schedule at the end, once the flow already works.
tasks.expect: A single box on the canvas, with the lightning bolt and the text 'When clicking Test workflow'. If you hover over it you'll see a small round '+' to its right: that's where the next box will hang from.
tasks.stuck: If you picked another trigger by mistake, click on the box to select it (it gets a border). Then press Delete. The canvas goes back to empty with its dashed box. It won't let you place two triggers of the same type in the same flow, and that's normal.

tasks.title: Add the box that brings in the outside data and run it
tasks.action: Hover over the trigger box and click the round '+' to its right. The 'What happens next?' panel opens with a search bar at the top. Type HTTP and pick 'HTTP Request'. The three-column view opens. On the left, INPUT (what arrives); in the center, the box's settings; on the right, OUTPUT (what comes out). Leave 'Method' on GET, which means 'I'm only going to look, not change anything'. In the 'URL' field paste this address: https://api.frankfurter.app/latest?from=USD&to=EUR . It's a public window that returns the official European Central Bank exchange rate, it's free and doesn't ask for registration or a key. Now click the 'Test step' button above the center column. When the result shows up on the right, switch that column's view from 'Table' to 'JSON' with the little buttons at the top. I want you to see the card as it really is.
tasks.prompt: I'm pasting the data card that an HTTP Request node in n8n returned to me. Explain it to me field by field, in plain English, as if I'd never seen data like this before. For each field tell me three things: what it means, whether it's text or a number, and whether it's nested inside another field or standalone. At the end, tell me the exact path I need to write in an n8n expression to grab the euro exchange rate value, in the format {{ $json.something }}, and explain in one line why that path and not another. Here's the card: [paste here what you see in the OUTPUT column with the view set to JSON]
tasks.expect: The OUTPUT column fills in and a card shows up that looks like this. It brings amount 1, base USD and date with today's date or the last business day. Inside rates, an EUR with a number like 0.9174. Above the column it'll say '1 item'. A green mark appears in the corner of the box.
tasks.stuck: If a red box shows up mentioning 'ENOTFOUND' or 'getaddrinfo', the address is misspelled. Check that the s in https isn't missing and that there's no extra space at the end. Also check that a line break hasn't sneaked in when you pasted. If you get a 403 or 404, that service has changed address. To keep going with the lesson use this other one instead, which returns data just as well: https://api.github.com/repos/n8n-io/n8n and look inside for the stargazers_count field. If the wheel just spins and nothing happens, your office network is probably blocking outbound connections. Try from a different connection or share your phone's data.

tasks.title: Pull the data out of the card and write the sentence with an expression
tasks.action: Go back to the canvas with 'Back to canvas' top left. Click the '+' to the right of the HTTP Request box, search for 'Edit Fields' and pick 'Edit Fields (Set)'. Leave 'Mode' on 'Manual Mapping' and click 'Add Field'. In 'Name' type: message. In 'Type' leave 'String', which means text. Now here's the important part: hover over the value field and you'll see a small pair of tabs appear, 'Fixed' and 'Expression'. Click 'Expression'. The field changes appearance and now accepts slots with data. Type inside: Today 1 dollar is worth {{ $json.rates.EUR }} euros. Data from {{ $json.date }}. Below the field, in gray, you'll see the sentence already resolved with the real number. There's an even better shortcut and I want you to try it. Delete what you wrote. From the INPUT column on the left, drag the EUR field and drop it inside the slot. n8n writes the expression for you, without you having to remember the path. Click 'Test step'.
tasks.prompt: I'm in an 'Edit Fields (Set)' node in n8n and I want to build a text that mixes my own words with data coming from the previous node. Here's the card that arrives: [paste the JSON from the INPUT column here]. I want the final text to say exactly this: 'Today 1 dollar is worth X euros. Data from Y.' where X is the exchange rate with two decimals and Y is the date in day/month/year format. Write me the complete expression ready to copy and paste, with the double curly braces where they belong. If I need to round the number or change the date format, do it inside the expression itself and explain in one line what each part does. Don't suggest a Code node: I want it resolved inside the field.
tasks.expect: Below the field, in gray, the finished sentence with the real number: 'Today 1 dollar is worth 0.9174 euros. Data from 2026-08-18.' And in the OUTPUT column, a single card with a single label called message and your sentence inside.
tasks.stuck: If the preview shows [undefined], the path doesn't exist: undefined means 'there's nothing here'. Count the levels by looking at the INPUT column. The number is inside rates, that's why it's two steps, $json.rates.EUR, and not $json.EUR. If it shows [Error], check that there are two braces on each side, {{ and }}, and that you haven't left one out. If the field won't let you type braces and treats them as plain text, you're still on the 'Fixed' tab: switch to 'Expression'.

tasks.title: Ask AI for the whole flow and paste it onto the canvas
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, and then in the n8n tab
tasks.action: An n8n flow is text underneath, and the canvas accepts you pasting that text directly. Copy the prompt below into your AI's message box and send it. When it replies, select the response from the first opening brace { to the last closing brace } and copy it. Go back to n8n and create a new flow with 'Create Workflow', so you don't overwrite the one you already have. Click anywhere empty on the canvas so the screen has focus. Then press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac). The boxes appear drawn and connected. Open them one by one and compare them with the ones you built by hand: you'll see they do exactly the same thing.
tasks.prompt: Generate an n8n flow ready to paste onto the canvas. Return ONLY the flow's JSON, starting with { and ending with }, with no explanation before or after and no code block markers. Requirements: 1) Use only basic nodes that definitely exist: Schedule Trigger, HTTP Request, and Edit Fields (Set). No community nodes or integrations that require an account. 2) The Schedule Trigger fires every day at 8:00. 3) The HTTP Request makes a GET request to https://api.frankfurter.app/latest?from=USD&to=EUR with no authentication. 4) The Edit Fields creates a text field called message whose value is: Today 1 dollar is worth {{ $json.rates.EUR }} euros. 5) The three nodes connected in that order. Give each node a name in English that's clear at a glance. If you're not sure about a parameter, leave it at its default value instead of making it up.
tasks.expect: Three new boxes drawn on the canvas and connected by arrows, with the names you asked for. If instead absolutely nothing happens, or you get a warning that it can't paste, what you copied wasn't the drawing.
tasks.stuck: The number one mistake is copying too much: you grab the code block's backticks or a courtesy sentence along with it. Copy only from the first brace to the last. Mistake number two is the AI inventing a node or a field. You'll see it right away: the box shows up with a warning triangle or its name in red. Don't fight it; delete that box and build it by hand like in the earlier tasks, which you already know how to do.

tasks.title: Swap the button for a schedule and truly activate the flow
tasks.where: In n8n, in your 'Dollar-euro rate every morning' flow
tasks.action: Click on the 'When clicking Test workflow' box and press Delete to remove it. Now click the '+' that appears top right of the canvas, search for 'Schedule Trigger' and pick it. Inside: under 'Trigger Interval' pick 'Days' and leave 'Days Between Triggers' at 1. Set 'Trigger at Hour' to 8am and 'Trigger at Minute' to 0. Go back to the canvas and connect the new box to HTTP Request. Drag from the gray dot on the right side of the schedule box to the dot on the left side of HTTP Request. Before activating, check the time: click the three dots '...' top right, go into 'Settings' and look at 'Timezone'. If it says America/New_York, your eight in the morning is two in the afternoon in Madrid; change it to Europe/Madrid and save. Click 'Save'. And now, click the switch that says 'Inactive' top right.
tasks.expect: The switch turns green and changes to 'Active'. A window pops up warning that from now on the flow runs on its own. You'll see each run in the 'Executions' tab. If you go back to Overview, your flow shows up with the green active tag.
tasks.stuck: If the switch won't move and you get a warning like 'Workflow could not be activated', it's almost always because you left the manual trigger in place. A flow that waits for you to press a button can't be turned on by itself. Delete it and leave only the schedule one. If nothing has run by 8:00 tomorrow and you have n8n on your computer, you already know the explanation. Active means active while the computer is on and the black window is open.

tasks.title: Break it on purpose and learn to read the failure
tasks.action: This isn't a whim: the only way to lose your fear of errors is to cause one on purpose while nothing is at stake. Open the HTTP Request box and remove a letter from the address, for example leave https://api.frankfurter.ap/latest?from=USD&to=EUR . Go back to the canvas with 'Back to canvas' and click 'Test workflow' at the bottom center. The box will turn red with a triangle. Click on it: the column on the right, where the card used to show up, is now a red box with the error message. Read it in full even if it's in English. Notice that the previous box is still green: that tells you exactly where the flow died. Now go up to the 'Executions' tab: that's the list of every time it's run, with the time and the result. Click the red line and you'll see the drawing frozen exactly as it was at that moment. Go back to the Editor, fix the letter you removed, save, and test again.
tasks.prompt: An n8n flow is failing on me and I want to understand it, not have it fixed blindly. I'm giving you three things and asking for three things back. What I'm giving you: (1) the red error message copied in full exactly as shown: [paste here]; (2) the node where it fails and what it has configured: [node name, method, address, any fields you touched]; (3) the card that arrived as input, copied from the INPUT column: [paste here]. What I'm asking for: first, translate the error into plain English in a single sentence; second, tell me the most likely cause and how to confirm it on screen, pointing me to exactly where to look; third, give me the fix, naming the exact field to touch and what to type. If there are several possible causes, order them from most to least likely. Don't suggest reinstalling anything or switching tools.
tasks.expect: First, a red box and an error message you can read and paste to the AI. After fixing the letter, the three boxes with their green mark and an item count above each arrow.
tasks.stuck: If it's still all red after fixing it, check that you actually pressed 'Test workflow' again. What you're seeing in the columns might be the frozen result from the previous run. If the error mentions 'JSON parameter needs to be valid JSON', you've touched a field that expected a well-formed card. It's missing a comma or a quote. And if you don't understand the message even with the translation, paste it in full with the prompt above. n8n errors are long, but they always tell you the node and the reason.

matters: Checking the INPUT and OUTPUT columns of each box. It's the only repair technique that exists in n8n and it replaces searching Google. Whoever ignores it spends the whole afternoon changing things at random in the node that failed. And the missing piece of data was lost two boxes earlier.

Understanding that save, test, and activate are three different buttons. A saved, tested flow doesn't run on its own; it needs the Active switch turned green and an automatic trigger. Ignoring this means finding out a week later that your perfect automation hasn't run even once.

Being the first recipient of everything the flow sends while you test it. Outside the editor there's no undo: sent emails, published messages, and deleted rows don't come back. A poorly closed loop can fire off thousands of executions in minutes, and it never happens to anyone twice, but the first time hurts.

Always saving access keys as a credential and never typing them by hand into a text field. Credentials are encrypted and don't go out inside the flow when you share it. A key typed by hand does travel inside the file. The day you send it by email, the only fix will be to revoke that key and get another one.
ignore: The whole node catalog. You'll see hundreds of names in the search bar, from Salesforce to Pinecone, and you don't need any of them yet. With four boxes you can build almost everything you'll need this month. They are the trigger, HTTP Request, Edit Fields, and If.

The Code node, the one that lets you write instructions inside it. Almost everything you think needs code gets solved with a two-brace expression, in the field you already have in front of you. An expression gets fixed by looking at the preview; a broken piece of code doesn't.

Anything that sounds like serious production: Docker on a real server, queues, workers, environment variables, and role-based permissions. Also AI Agent nodes with memory. That comes when one of your flows becomes critical to someone's money, and you'll know that day when it arrives.
canDo: Write you the exact expression to pull a piece of data out of the card, if you paste it the JSON you see in the input column. It can even round a number or format a date the way you want.
Translate the red error message for you and tell you the most likely cause. That said, give it the full error, the node where it happened, and the card that arrived.
Give you the whole flow as text so you can paste it onto the canvas with Ctrl+V. The boxes show up already connected and you save yourself a quarter hour of dragging and searching.
Design the flow from a plain-language description of yours. It'll tell you which boxes you need, in what order, and where it makes sense to add a check before sending anything.
cantDo: Press buttons for you. It doesn't create your account, doesn't connect your Gmail, and doesn't accept the credential notice. And it certainly doesn't flip the Activate switch. All of that is on you, with the mouse.

Know which nodes and fields your specific version of n8n has. It invents names with total confidence, because the tool changes faster than it learns. That's why you should ask it for basic nodes and check every box after pasting it.
Guess why something is failing if you don't show it the evidence. Without the copied error and the input card, it'll give you five generic causes and none of them will be yours.

See what's inside your spreadsheet, your inbox, or your account on some service. It only knows what you paste into the message. If the flow breaks because of an empty row at row 340, you have to show it that row.
words: Node
Each box in the drawing. A box does exactly one thing: check the time, ask another program for a piece of data, decide between two paths, or send an alert.
Flow (workflow)
The whole drawing, with all its boxes and arrows, saved under a name. It's what you turn on or off.
Trigger
The very first box, the one that decides when everything else starts. It can be a fixed time, an email arriving, someone filling out a form, or you pressing a button.
Execution
One full run of the drawing, from the first box to the last. Even with twenty boxes it counts as a single one, and it's the unit you get billed by.
JSON
The data card that passes from box to box: labels on the left, values on the right, all inside curly braces. It's pronounced 'jay-sahn'.
Expression

A slot where you don't type a fixed value, but the instruction to go fetch it from the card that just arrived. It's written between double curly braces and n8n shows you the real result underneath as you type.
Credential
The key to another service, typed once and kept separately under lock. All your drawings can use it without it appearing written inside them.
API
The window through which one program lets other programs request data directly, without a person filling anything in. The currency exchange window you use in this lesson is one of them.
Webhook
An internet address your drawing sits there listening on. You give it to another program so it can notify you the moment something happens. That way you don't have to keep asking every five minutes.
localhost
The name your own computer has when seen from inside itself. An address that starts with that only works on your machine and no one outside can open it.
next: In the next lesson you'll attach the last box to the flow: getting that piece of data to your phone or email on its own every morning, and having the flow itself warn you the day it breaks.
